summary: Records that the Unicode Consortium deprecated the language tag characters described in RFC 2482 and recommends against their use, and moves RFC 2482 to Historic status to reduce the chance people use it.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2482 proposed special Unicode characters for identifying a language in plain text. RFC 6082 records that the Unicode Consortium deprecated this method and moves RFC 2482 to Historic status.

questions: why was rfc 2482 moved to historic
subtitle: Moves the Unicode language tag character facility in RFC 2482 to Historic status.

tldr.problem: RFC 2482 described Unicode language tag characters, but the Unicode Consortium deprecated the facility and strongly recommended against using it.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6082 reclassifies RFC 2482 as Historic and tells Internet protocols and Standards-Track documents not to use its facilities.
tldr.outcome: RFC 6082 is an informational notice intended to reduce the chance that implementers choose the deprecated language-tag mechanism.

today: RFC 6082 is informational. It records that RFC 2482 is Historic and that protocols and Standards-Track documents should not use the language tag character facility.

sections.title: The Deprecated Language Tag Characters
sections.content:
RFC 2482 describes special Unicode language tag characters that could identify the language of text without general markup such as XML. RFC 6082 says the Unicode Consortium deprecated the facility and strongly recommended against its use.

The memo points to whole-transaction language identification, such as the MIME Content-Language header, and general markup mechanisms such as XML as other approaches.
sections.plainLanguage: RFC 2482 proposed special characters to label text with its language. The Unicode Consortium no longer recommends that method.

sections.title: Action for Protocol Designers
sections.content:
RFC 2482 is deprecated and reclassified as Historic. Internet protocols and Standards-Track documents should not use the facilities it describes.

The stated purpose is to reduce the chance that Internet implementers will consider the language-tag character system appropriate for identifying languages.
sections.plainLanguage: New Internet protocols should not use the language-tag characters described in RFC 2482. The Historic status is intended to discourage that choice.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The memo says the facility may have been slightly risky if it was misinterpreted or if expected support was not available. It states that any effect of this action on Internet security should be positive.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC says misinterpretation or missing support could create a small risk. Retiring the facility is expected to help rather than harm security.

references.text: Whistler, K. and G. Adams, "Language Tagging in Unicode Plain Text", RFC 2482, January 1999.
Alvestrand, H., "Content Language Headers", RFC 3282, May 2002.
